blocks.content: A container's exit code, visible in docker ps -a, is often the fastest clue to why it stopped, before you even open the logs.
1. Where the Exit Code Shows Up
blocks.text: 1. Where the Exit Code Shows Up

blocks.content: docker ps -a shows a stopped container's exit code right in its status column, a quick glance here often narrows down the category of problem before reading a single line of log output.

blocks.alt: Visible immediately, before digging into logs at all

blocks.content:
docker ps -a
# STATUS
# Exited (1) 2 minutes ago

code.content:
docker ps -a
# STATUS
# Exited (1) 2 minutes ago

codes.bash:
docker ps -a
# STATUS
# Exited (1) 2 minutes ago

blocks.content: 2. The Codes Worth Recognizing on Sight
blocks.text: 2. The Codes Worth Recognizing on Sight

blocks.content: A handful of exit codes come up constantly: 0 means a clean, intentional exit, 1 is a generic application error (the logs will have the real detail), and two codes specifically correspond to the process being killed by a signal rather than exiting on its own.

blocks.alt: A handful of codes cover most real situations

blocks.content: {"headers":["Exit Code","Meaning"],"rows":[["0","Clean, successful exit"],["1","Generic application error, check the logs for detail"],["126","Command found but not executable, a permissions issue"],["127","Command not found at all, likely a typo or missing binary"],["137","Killed with SIGKILL, very often an out-of-memory kill"],["143","Killed with SIGTERM, often a normal docker stop"]]}

These numbers are not arbitrary, they follow a real convention: 128 plus the signal number. 137 is 128 + 9 (SIGKILL), and is very frequently the signature of an OOM kill, exactly the mechanism covered in the Resource Limits and cgroups topics. 143 is 128 + 15 (SIGTERM), commonly just an ordinary, graceful docker stop.

blocks.alt: 137 specifically is a strong signal to check memory limits first

blocks.content:
docker inspect web --format='{{.State.OOMKilled}}'
# true confirms exit code 137 was specifically an OOM kill

code.content:
docker inspect web --format='{{.State.OOMKilled}}'
# true confirms exit code 137 was specifically an OOM kill

codes.bash:
docker inspect web --format='{{.State.OOMKilled}}'
# true confirms exit code 137 was specifically an OOM kill

blocks.content: These two are specifically about the command itself: 126 means the command exists but could not be executed (often a missing execute permission), 127 means the shell could not find the command at all, commonly a typo in CMD/ENTRYPOINT or a binary that genuinely is not present in the image.

blocks.alt: Both point directly at a problem with the command itself

blocks.content: 5. Using the Code to Direct Your Next Step
blocks.text: 5. Using the Code to Direct Your Next Step

blocks.content: The exit code should shape where you look next, a 137 sends you straight to checking memory limits and OOM status, while a 1 sends you straight to the application's own logs for the real, specific error message.

blocks.alt: The exit code points you at the right next debugging step

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: A container's exit code, visible in docker ps -a, is often the fastest first clue to what went wrong, before reading any logs.
137 (SIGKILL, often OOM) and 143 (SIGTERM, often a normal stop) are worth recognizing on sight, they point to very different root causes.
